name: SUM

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range to add.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Adds all the numbers in a range of cells.
intro: SUM is the most-used function in Excel. It adds numbers in cells, ranges, or a mix of both — and it ignores text and empty cells, so you can select an entire column without cleaning it first.

examples.title: Sum a column
examples.note: A contiguous range is the fastest way to total a column.

examples.title: Sum individual cells
examples.note: Separate non-adjacent cells with commas.

commonErrors.cause: A referenced cell contains an error or text that can't be read as a number.
commonErrors.fix: Check the range for error values like #DIV/0! and fix those first.

name: COUNT

params.name: value1
params.description: The first item or range to count.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional items or ranges.

summary: Counts how many cells in a range contain numbers.
intro: COUNT tells you how many cells in a range hold numeric values. Text, blanks and logical values are skipped — use COUNTA instead if you need to count non-empty cells of any type.

examples.title: Count ignores text
examples.note: Only the numeric cell is counted.

name: COUNTA

params.name: value1
params.description: The first cell or range to count.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional cells or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Counts how many cells in a range are not empty.
intro: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell — numbers, text, dates, errors and even formulas that return an empty string. It is the quickest way to check how much data a column actually holds, which makes it ideal for validating imports and form responses.

examples.title: Count filled cells
examples.note: The blank cell is skipped; text and numbers both count.

examples.title: Check a form column is complete
examples.note: Pair COUNTA with IF to flag incomplete lists.

commonErrors.cause: Cells containing spaces or formulas returning "" are not empty.
commonErrors.fix: Use TRIM to remove stray spaces, or COUNTBLANK to find visually-empty cells.

name: AVERAGE

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range to average.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges.

summary: Returns the average (arithmetic mean) of its arguments.
intro: AVERAGE adds up the numeric cells in a range and divides by how many there are. Like SUM, it ignores text and empty cells — but a 0 counts, so a blank and a zero give different results.

examples.title: Average with a blank cell
examples.note: The blank is skipped entirely — the divisor is 2, not 3.

commonErrors.cause: The range contains no numeric values.
commonErrors.fix: Make sure at least one cell in the range holds a number.

name: VLOOKUP

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to search for in the first column of the table.

params.name: table_array
params.description: The range of cells that contains the data.

params.name: col_index_num
params.description: The column number (counting from the left of table_array) to return.

params.name: range_lookup
params.description: TRUE for approximate match, FALSE for exact. Defaults to TRUE.

summary: Looks up a value in the first column of a table and returns a value in the same row from another column.
intro: VLOOKUP is Excel's classic lookup function: give it a key and a table, and it walks down the first column until it finds a match, then returns the value from whichever column number you specify. It is fast to write but has two famous limits — it can only look to the right, and a hard-coded column index breaks when you insert columns. For new workbooks, XLOOKUP or INDEX+MATCH are more flexible.

examples.title: Find a product price
examples.note: FALSE forces an exact match — always use it for IDs and SKUs.

examples.title: Approximate match on a grade table
examples.note: TRUE finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup; the first column must be sorted ascending.

examples.title: Lookup across sheets
examples.note: Prefix the range with SheetName! to pull from another worksheet.

commonErrors.cause: The lookup value is not in the first column — often due to extra spaces or mismatched types (number vs text).
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the value in TRIM, or use IFERROR to catch the miss.

commonErrors.cause: col_index_num is bigger than the number of columns in table_array.
commonErrors.fix: Check that the index counts from the leftmost column of the lookup range, not of the sheet.

commonErrors.cause: range_lookup was left as TRUE so Excel returned an approximate match.
commonErrors.fix: Add FALSE as the fourth argument for exact matching.

name: XLOOKUP

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to search for.

params.name: lookup_array
params.description: The range or array to search.

params.name: return_array
params.description: The range or array to return a value from.

params.name: if_not_found
params.description: Text or value to return instead of #N/A when nothing matches.

params.name: match_mode
params.description: 0 = exact (default), -1 = exact or next smaller, 1 = exact or next larger, 2 = wildcard.

params.name: search_mode
params.description: 1 = first to last (default), -1 = last to first, 2/-2 = binary search.

summary: Searches a range and returns an item from a second range — the modern replacement for VLOOKUP.
intro: XLOOKUP fixes nearly every VLOOKUP limitation: it searches any column (not just the leftmost), returns from a separate range so inserting columns never breaks it, defaults to exact match, can search right-to-left, and has a built-in 'if not found' message. It requires Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+.

examples.title: Look up to the left
examples.note: The return column sits left of the lookup column — impossible with VLOOKUP.

examples.title: Custom not-found message
examples.note: No IFERROR wrapper needed.

examples.title: Return a whole row
examples.note: A multi-column return_array spills results into neighbouring cells.

commonErrors.cause: No match and no if_not_found argument was supplied.
commonErrors.fix: Add a fourth argument like "Not found" to make misses readable.

commonErrors.cause: lookup_array and return_array have different sizes.
commonErrors.fix: Make both ranges the same length (e.g. A2:A10 and B2:B10).

commonErrors.cause: The workbook runs in Excel 2019 or earlier, which lacks XLOOKUP.
commonErrors.fix: Use INDEX+MATCH or VLOOKUP for older versions.

name: INDEX

params.name: array
params.description: The range of cells or array constant to pick from.

params.name: row_num
params.description: The row position within array to return.

params.name: column_num
params.description: The column position within array to return.

summary: Returns the value at a given row and column position inside a range.
intro: INDEX does one thing perfectly: it fetches the cell at position (row, column) of a range. On its own it is a simple coordinate picker; combined with MATCH — which finds the position of a value — it becomes the most flexible lookup pattern in Excel, able to look left, right, up or down.

examples.title: Two-dimensional lookup
examples.note: Row 2 of the range is 'South', column 2 is 'Feb'.

examples.title: INDEX + MATCH lookup
examples.note: MATCH finds the row; INDEX returns the price. No column-index to break.

commonErrors.cause: row_num or column_num points outside the array.
commonErrors.fix: Check that positions are relative to the array, not the worksheet.

name: MATCH

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to locate.

params.name: lookup_array
params.description: The single row or column range to search.

params.name: match_type
params.description: 1 = largest value ≤ lookup (sorted asc), 0 = exact, -1 = smallest ≥ lookup (sorted desc).

summary: Finds the position of a value inside a row or column.
intro: MATCH returns a number — the relative position of your lookup value in a range — rather than the value itself. That position is exactly what INDEX needs, which is why INDEX+MATCH is the classic flexible lookup pair. Use match_type 0 for exact matches; 1 and -1 require sorted data.

examples.title: Find the position of a name
Approximate position in sorted prices
examples.note: match_type 1 returns the largest value that is ≤ 40.

commonErrors.cause: No exact match exists, or the list is not sorted for match_type 1/-1.
commonErrors.fix: For exact lookups keep match_type 0; for approximate, sort the lookup array correctly.

name: IF

params.name: logical_test
params.description: Any expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

params.name: value_if_true
params.description: What to return when the test is TRUE.

params.name: value_if_false
params.description: What to return when the test is FALSE (defaults to FALSE).

summary: Returns one value if a condition is true and another if it is false.
intro: IF is the decision-maker of Excel: test a condition, return A when it holds and B when it does not. Nest IFs for more than two outcomes — or reach for IFS, which reads like a flat list of conditions and is far easier to audit.

examples.title: Nested IF for three grades
examples.note: For many branches, IFS is cleaner.

commonErrors.cause: Text compared with = is not case-sensitive, and numbers stored as text fail numeric tests.
commonErrors.fix: Convert text numbers with VALUE or check LEN/TRIM issues first.

commonErrors.cause: The logical test references an error cell.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the test with IFERROR.

name: IFS

params.name: logical_test1
params.description: The first condition to evaluate.

params.name: value_if_true1
params.description: Result returned when the first condition is TRUE.

params.name: logical_testN
params.description: Additional test/result pairs, evaluated left to right.

summary: Evaluates multiple conditions and returns the value for the first TRUE one.
intro: IFS replaces deeply nested IF statements with a flat list of test/result pairs. Excel stops at the first TRUE condition, so order your tests from most to least specific. Available in Excel 2019 and Microsoft 365 — for a final catch-all, end with TRUE as the last test.

examples.title: Grade bands
examples.note: The trailing TRUE acts as 'else'.

commonErrors.cause: No condition evaluated to TRUE.
commonErrors.fix: Add a final TRUE,default-value pair as a fallback.

commonErrors.cause: IFS does not exist in Excel 2016 or earlier.
commonErrors.fix: Rewrite as nested IF.

name: SUMIF

params.name: range
params.description: The cells evaluated against criteria.

params.name: criteria
params.description: The condition, e.g. ">100", "apples" or a cell reference.

params.name: sum_range
params.description: The cells to actually add; defaults to range.

summary: Adds the cells that meet a single condition.
intro: SUMIF sums only the rows that satisfy one test — 'add up sales for the East region', 'total invoices over $500'. The criteria range and the sum range can be different columns, which makes it perfect for category totals. When you need two or more conditions, step up to SUMIFS.

examples.title: Sum values above a threshold
examples.note: When sum_range is omitted, range is summed.

commonErrors.cause: sum_range is a different size than range — Excel silently shifts it.
commonErrors.fix: Keep sum_range the same shape and starting row as range.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria type mismatch, e.g. comparing numbers stored as text.
commonErrors.fix: Normalize the column type (Text to Columns or VALUE).

name: SUMIFS

params.name: sum_range
params.description: The cells to add.

params.name: criteria_range1
params.description: The first range to test.

params.name: criteria1
params.description: The condition applied to criteria_range1.

params.name: criteria_range2 / criteria2
params.description: Extra range/condition pairs — all must be TRUE.

summary: Adds the cells that meet several conditions at once.
intro: SUMIFS extends SUMIF to as many criteria pairs as you need — 'total sales for East AND January', 'invoices over $500 AND unpaid'. Note the argument order differs from SUMIF: the range to sum comes first. Every criteria range must be the same size as sum_range.

examples.title: Amount in a date window
examples.note: Two criteria on the same range create a between filter.

commonErrors.cause: A criteria range does not match sum_range's dimensions.
commonErrors.fix: Every criteria_range must have the same number of rows/columns as sum_range.

name: COUNTIF

params.name: range
params.description: The cells to evaluate.

params.name: criteria
params.description: The condition, e.g. "yes", ">=10" or a cell reference.

summary: Counts the cells that meet a single condition.
intro: COUNTIF answers 'how many?' with one condition — how many orders say 'shipped', how many scores beat 80, how many times a name appears (the classic duplicate check). Criteria support wildcards (* and ?) and comparison operators, which makes it far more flexible than a plain COUNT.

examples.title: Duplicate flag
examples.note: TRUE means the name in A1 appears more than once.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria contain leading/trailing spaces or the column mixes text and numbers.
commonErrors.fix: TRIM the data or match the cell's stored type.

name: COUNTIFS

params.name: criteria_range1
params.description: The first range to test.

params.name: criteria1
params.description: The condition applied to criteria_range1.

params.name: criteria_range2 / criteria2
params.description: Additional range/condition pairs — all must be TRUE.

summary: Counts the rows that meet several conditions at once.
intro: COUNTIFS is the multi-test version of COUNTIF: every pair adds an AND filter, so 'count East rows in January that are over $100' is one formula. It is the fastest way to sanity-check a filtered export without leaving the grid.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria ranges have different sizes.
commonErrors.fix: Every criteria_range must span the same number of cells.

name: LEFT

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to slice.

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to take from the start; defaults to 1.

summary: Returns the first characters of a text string.
intro: LEFT grabs a fixed-length prefix — the first 3 characters of a product code, the area code of a phone number, the first word when paired with FIND. Text functions return text, so wrap LEFT in VALUE when you need the number back.

examples.title: First word of a name
examples.note: FIND locates the space; subtracting 1 drops it from the result.

commonErrors.cause: Hidden spaces or non-printing characters inflate the prefix.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap text in TRIM/CLEAN first.

name: RIGHT

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to slice.

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to take from the end; defaults to 1.

summary: Returns the last characters of a text string.
intro: RIGHT pulls a suffix — file extensions, last-4 digits of an ID, the postal code at the end of an address. Combined with LEN and FIND it extracts everything after a delimiter, which is the standard way to get the last word of a phrase in older Excel versions.

examples.title: Text after the hyphen
examples.note: LEN minus the delimiter position gives the suffix length.

commonErrors.cause: num_chars counts characters, not words.
commonErrors.fix: Use LEN(text)-FIND(...) to compute the right length.

name: MID

params.name: text
params.description: The text string to slice.

params.name: start_num
params.description: The position of the first character to return (1-based).

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to return.

summary: Returns characters from the middle of a text string.
intro: MID is the scalpel of the text functions: start anywhere, take any length. It shines when the piece you need sits between two markers — extract the domain after '@', the middle segment of a code, or characters at a computed position from FIND.

commonErrors.cause: start_num is beyond the string's length.
commonErrors.fix: Guard with IF(start_num<=LEN(text), ...) or check with LEN first.

name: LEN

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to measure.

summary: Returns the number of characters in a text string.
intro: LEN counts every character — including trailing spaces you cannot see. That makes it the best debugging tool for 'the VLOOKUP should have matched but didn't': a LEN of 9 on an 8-character SKU means stray whitespace, and TRIM is the fix.

examples.title: Spot hidden spaces
examples.note: The difference reveals one trailing space.

commonErrors.cause: LEN counts spaces and non-breaking spaces.
commonErrors.fix: TRIM removes regular spaces; SUBSTITUTE with CHAR(160) handles non-breaking ones.

name: TRIM

params.name: text
params.description: The text to clean.

summary: Removes leading, trailing and repeated inner spaces from text.
intro: TRIM strips the invisible clutter that breaks lookups and comparisons: leading spaces, trailing spaces, and double spaces between words. Run it on imported data before any VLOOKUP or COUNTIF — mismatched whitespace is the #1 cause of 'value exists but lookup fails'.

examples.title: Fix a lookup
examples.note: After TRIM, the padded key matches.

commonErrors.cause: The cells contain non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)), common in web pastes.
commonErrors.fix: Use TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A1,CHAR(160)," ")).

name: CONCAT

params.name: text1
params.description: The first text item or range to join.

params.name: text2
params.description: Additional text items or ranges (up to 253).

summary: Joins text items and ranges into one string — no delimiter support.
intro: CONCAT is the modern successor to CONCATENATE: it accepts whole ranges as well as individual cells, so =CONCAT(A1:C1) joins a row without listing each cell. It inserts nothing between items — when you need commas, spaces or a 'skip blanks' switch, use TEXTJOIN instead.

commonErrors.cause: The workbook runs in Excel 2016 or earlier.
commonErrors.fix: Use CONCATENATE or the & operator.

commonErrors.cause: CONCAT adds no separator between items.
commonErrors.fix: Insert literal separators (", ") or switch to TEXTJOIN.

name: TEXTJOIN

params.name: delimiter
params.description: The separator placed between each item, e.g. ", ".

params.name: ignore_empty
params.description: TRUE skips empty cells; FALSE keeps them.

params.name: text1
params.description: The first text item or range.

params.name: text2
params.description: Additional items or ranges.

summary: Joins text with a chosen delimiter and can skip empty cells.
intro: TEXTJOIN is CONCAT with manners: a real delimiter and an ignore_empty flag that prevents stray commas when the list has gaps. It is the go-to for building CSV rows, combining address parts, or producing 'A, B, C' lists from a column — all without helper cells.

examples.title: Skip the blanks
examples.note: With FALSE you'd get a double comma.

commonErrors.cause: TEXTJOIN requires Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.
commonErrors.fix: Fall back to CONCAT with manual delimiters.

commonErrors.cause: The joined result exceeds the 32,767 character cell limit.
commonErrors.fix: Join fewer items or split the output.

name: TODAY
summary: Returns the current date, refreshed every recalculation.
intro: TODAY() returns the system date — no arguments. Because it recalculates whenever the workbook opens or changes, it powers rolling reports like 'invoices due in the next 7 days' or 'days since signup'. For a frozen timestamp, use Ctrl+; instead.

examples.title: Days overdue
examples.result: Number of days between the due date and today
examples.note: Format the result as General, not Date.

examples.title: Flag items older than 30 days
examples.note: The serial date in A1 stands in for any past date.

commonErrors.error: Result shows a date, not a number
commonErrors.cause: Subtracting dates inherits date formatting.
commonErrors.fix: Set the cell format to General or Number.

name: NOW
summary: Returns the current date and time, refreshed on every recalculation.
intro: NOW() is TODAY() with the clock attached — date plus time as a serial number. Use it for timestamps on logs, 'last refreshed' stamps on dashboards, or elapsed-time calculations. Remember it is volatile: the value updates at every recalc, so paste-values if you need to freeze it.

examples.title: Current timestamp
examples.note: Displays like 11/9/2026 17:43 depending on formatting.

examples.title: Hours since an event
examples.note: Multiply the day-fraction difference by 24.

commonErrors.cause: The cell is formatted as a number.
commonErrors.fix: Format as 'm/d/yyyy h:mm'.

name: DATE

params.name: year
params.description: A four-digit year.

params.name: month
params.description: Month number; values >12 roll into the next year.

params.name: day
params.description: Day number; values >month length roll forward.

summary: Builds a valid date from separate year, month and day values.
intro: DATE assembles a serial date from parts — essential when a system exports year, month and day as separate columns, or when you compute dates like 'the last day of next month' (=DATE(y, m+2, 0)). Its rollover behaviour is a feature: month 13 becomes January of the following year.

examples.title: Last day of next month
examples.note: Day 0 rolls back to the last day of the previous month.

commonErrors.cause: Two-digit years map to 1900s (e.g. 26 → 1926).
commonErrors.fix: Always pass a four-digit year.

commonErrors.cause: An argument is text rather than a number.
commonErrors.fix: Convert with VALUE or check the source column type.

name: DATEDIF

params.name: start_date
params.description: The earlier date.

params.name: end_date
params.description: The later date.

params.name: unit
params.description: "Y" years, "M" months, "D" days, "MD"/"YM"/"YD" partial variants.

summary: Calculates the difference between two dates in years, months or days.
intro: DATEDIF is a hidden gem — it exists in every Excel version but never appears in the function list. Feed it two dates and a unit code to compute ages ('Y'), contract lengths ('M') or 'days between'. The 'MD' unit has known quirks; prefer 'D' for plain day counts.

commonErrors.cause: start_date is after end_date.
commonErrors.fix: Swap the arguments or wrap in IFERROR.

commonErrors.cause: "MD" unit can return negative or wrong values in some builds.
commonErrors.fix: Use "D" and divide, or compute year/month separately.

name: MAX

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Returns the largest numeric value in a set.
intro: MAX scans a range and hands back the biggest number — top sales figure, latest serial date, highest score. Text and blanks are ignored, so it is safe over messy columns. For 'the Nth largest', use LARGE; for conditional maxima, MAXIFS or MAX + IF in older versions.

examples.title: MAX over mixed data
examples.note: Text is skipped entirely.

commonErrors.cause: All values are text or the range is empty.
commonErrors.fix: Convert stored-as-text numbers first.

name: MIN

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Returns the smallest numeric value in a set.
intro: MIN finds the floor of your data — lowest price, earliest serial date, minimum score. It pairs naturally with MAX to bracket a dataset, and with SMALL when you need the 2nd, 3rd or Nth lowest instead of the absolute minimum.

commonErrors.cause: All values are text or the range is empty.
commonErrors.fix: Convert stored-as-text numbers first.

name: LARGE

params.name: array
params.description: The range of numbers to rank.

params.name: k
params.description: The rank to return — 1 is the largest.

summary: Returns the k-th largest value in a set.
intro: LARGE answers 'top N' questions: the 2nd-biggest sale, the 3rd-highest score, the top-5 total when wrapped in SUM. It is the backbone of leaderboard formulas, and it ignores text and blanks so you can point it at a raw data column.

examples.title: Sum of top 3
examples.note: An array constant sums the top three in one step.

commonErrors.cause: k is bigger than the number of numeric values in array.
commonErrors.fix: Check COUNT(range) first, or clamp k.

name: SMALL

params.name: array
params.description: The range of numbers to rank.

params.name: k
params.description: The rank to return — 1 is the smallest.

summary: Returns the k-th smallest value in a set.
intro: SMALL is LARGE mirrored: it returns the Nth lowest value — second-cheapest price, third-shortest time. It is a quiet powerhouse for outlier hunting and 'bottom 10%' checks without sorting the sheet.

examples.title: Median via SMALL
examples.note: For odd-sized sets, k=(n+1)/2 gives the middle value.

commonErrors.cause: k exceeds the count of numeric entries.
commonErrors.fix: Compare k against COUNT(range) before ranking.

name: ROUND

params.name: number
params.description: The value to round.

params.name: num_digits
params.description: Digits to keep: 2 = cents, 0 = whole, -2 = hundreds.

summary: Rounds a number to a specified number of digits.
intro: ROUND actually changes the stored value — unlike cell formatting, which only changes how it displays. That distinction matters in money math: display-rounded cells can still sum to a wrong-looking total, while ROUNDed values add up exactly. Negative num_digits round left of the decimal point.

commonErrors.cause: Cells were display-rounded instead of ROUND-ed.
commonErrors.fix: Apply ROUND inside the formula before summing.

name: IFERROR

params.name: value
params.description: The formula or expression to evaluate.

params.name: value_if_error
params.description: What to return if value produces any error.

summary: Catches any formula error and returns a friendly fallback instead.
intro: IFERROR swallows #N/A, #DIV/0!, #REF!, #VALUE! and friends in one wrapper — the standard way to keep lookup misses and divide-by-zeros from wrecking a dashboard. Use it deliberately though: hiding every error can mask real data problems, so prefer fixing the root cause when you can.

commonErrors.cause: The wrapped formula itself is broken — IFERROR hides the clue.
commonErrors.fix: Remove IFERROR temporarily to see the real error.

name: TEXT

params.name: value
params.description: The number, date or value to format.

params.name: format_text
params.description: An Excel format code in quotes, e.g. "#,##0.00" or "mmmm yyyy".

summary: Converts a value to text in a specific number format.
intro: TEXT turns numbers and dates into formatted strings for concatenation: 'Total: $1,250.00', 'Due March 2027'. Once TEXT runs, the result is text — you cannot sum it — so apply it at the very last step, when a number becomes a message.

commonErrors.cause: Excel applies the workbook's locale — codes like "aaaa" mean "yyyy" in some locales.
commonErrors.fix: Use English format codes and test in the target locale.

commonErrors.cause: The format string is missing quotes.
commonErrors.fix: Always quote the format: TEXT(A1,"0.00").

name: FIND

params.name: find_text
params.description: The substring to locate.

params.name: within_text
params.description: The text to search.

params.name: start_num
params.description: The character position to start searching from; defaults to 1.

summary: Returns the starting position of a substring inside text.
intro: FIND is the case-sensitive counterpart to SEARCH: it reports exactly where a marker starts, which makes it the standard building block for extracting codes, domains and IDs with MID or LEFT. Pair it with LEN when you need the length of the text before a delimiter.

examples.title: Find an email domain marker
examples.note: Use the position with MID to return everything after the @.

commonErrors.cause: The substring is not present, or start_num is beyond the end of the text.
commonErrors.fix: Check spelling and case first; FIND is case-sensitive, unlike SEARCH.

commonErrors.cause: Excel positions start at 1, not 0.
commonErrors.fix: Subtract 1 only when you need a count of characters before the match.

name: SUBSTITUTE

params.name: text
params.description: The text to change.

params.name: old_text
params.description: The substring to find.

params.name: new_text
params.description: The replacement text.

params.name: instance_num
params.description: Which occurrence to replace; omit to replace all.

summary: Replaces one or more occurrences of text inside a string.
intro: SUBSTITUTE rewrites fragments without touching the rest of the string: swap date separators, remove a prefix, or replace only the second instance of a repeated token. It is case-sensitive and works on literal text, so it cannot match patterns the way wildcard criteria can.

examples.title: Replace only one occurrence
examples.note: instance_num 2 targets the middle a only.

commonErrors.cause: old_text does not match exactly, including case and spaces.
commonErrors.fix: Inspect the cell with LEN and TRIM; use UPPER/LOWER only if you intentionally normalize first.

commonErrors.cause: instance_num is larger than the number of matches.
commonErrors.fix: Remove instance_num to replace every occurrence, or verify the count.

name: UPPER

params.name: text
params.description: The text to convert to uppercase.

summary: Converts text to uppercase letters.
intro: UPPER normalizes casing before comparisons or displays, which is especially useful when imported data mixes 'East', 'EAST' and 'east'. It changes letters only — digits, punctuation and already-uppercase text pass through untouched.

commonErrors.cause: UPPER affects letters, not numeric values.
commonErrors.fix: If you need a formatted number, use TEXT instead.

commonErrors.cause: The other side of the comparison has different spacing or punctuation.
commonErrors.fix: Combine UPPER with TRIM before comparing.

name: LOWER

params.name: text
params.description: The text to convert to lowercase.

summary: Converts text to lowercase letters.
intro: LOWER is the gentler half of case normalization: it makes headings, codes and imported labels consistent without shouting. Use it before exact-match tests when the business rule is 'case does not matter', and remember the result is still text.

examples.title: Prepare a slug
examples.note: LOWER composes cleanly with SUBSTITUTE for simple slugs.

commonErrors.cause: LOWER leaves digits and symbols alone.
commonErrors.fix: Use VALUE or TEXT for numeric formatting.

commonErrors.cause: Whitespace or punctuation differs between the two values.
commonErrors.fix: Apply TRIM to both sides of the comparison.

name: PROPER

params.name: text
params.description: The text to capitalize.

summary: Capitalizes the first letter of each word and lowercases the rest.
intro: PROPER is built for names and titles that arrive as 'JOHN SMITH' or 'john smith'. It capitalizes after spaces and common separators, but it is not linguistically aware — names such as 'McDonald' can come back as 'Mcdonald', so review surnames before trusting it for formal output.

commonErrors.cause: PROPER applies a simple capitalization rule, not name rules.
commonErrors.fix: Manually correct exceptions or keep a lookup table for known names.

commonErrors.cause: PROPER lowercases interior capitals, so 'USA' can become 'Usa'.
commonErrors.fix: Restore acronyms with SUBSTITUTE or an IF check.

name: VALUE

params.name: text
params.description: Text that looks like a number, date or time.

summary: Converts a text representation of a number into a real number.
intro: VALUE rescues numbers trapped in imported text — '1,250.5', '42', or a date string — so SUM, AVERAGE and comparisons can use them. It is locale-sensitive for separators, and once the conversion succeeds the cell behaves like any other numeric value.

examples.title: Use the converted value in math
examples.note: The text '42' becomes the number 42 before the addition.

commonErrors.cause: The text cannot be interpreted as a number in the workbook locale.
commonErrors.fix: Check for letters, stray spaces or a different decimal separator.

commonErrors.cause: VALUE must be applied in a formula; the original text cell remains text.
commonErrors.fix: Create a helper column with =VALUE(A1) and copy-paste values back if needed.

name: HLOOKUP

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to find in the first row of table_array.

params.name: table_array
params.description: The range containing the lookup row and return rows.

params.name: row_index_num
params.description: The row number within table_array to return.

params.name: range_lookup
params.description: TRUE for approximate match, FALSE for exact; defaults to TRUE.

summary: Looks across the first row of a table and returns a value from the same column.
intro: HLOOKUP is VLOOKUP rotated ninety degrees: the search key sits across columns instead of down rows. It is handy for wide monthly grids, but the same cautions apply — hard-coded row indexes break when rows move, and approximate mode requires sorted data.

examples.title: Find February sales
examples.note: FALSE forces an exact match on the month header.

examples.title: Return a lower row
examples.note: Row index 3 counts from the top of the lookup range.

commonErrors.cause: The key is absent from the first row, or range_lookup is TRUE on unsorted data.
commonErrors.fix: Use FALSE for exact matches and TRIM/clean the header row.

commonErrors.cause: row_index_num is larger than the number of rows in table_array.
commonErrors.fix: Count rows inside the selected range, not on the worksheet.

commonErrors.cause: The first row has duplicate or visually similar headers.
commonErrors.fix: Make headers unique or use a key column with XLOOKUP.

name: FILTER

params.name: array
params.description: The range or array to return rows from.

params.name: include
params.description: A TRUE/FALSE array that selects rows.

params.name: if_empty
params.description: Value to return when no rows match.

summary: Returns only the rows of a range that meet a condition.
intro: FILTER is the formula version of AutoFilter: point it at a table, give it a Boolean test, and it spills the matching rows into the worksheet. It replaces fragile helper columns and is the fastest way to build dynamic summaries that update as source data changes.

examples.title: Sum East-region sales
examples.note: FILTER returns 100 and 80; SUM totals the spill.

examples.title: List matching labels
examples.note: TEXTJOIN collapses the spilled labels into one cell.

commonErrors.cause: No rows satisfy the include test and no if_empty value was supplied.
commonErrors.fix: Add a third argument such as "No matches" or IFERROR.

commonErrors.cause: The include array is not the same height or width as array.
commonErrors.fix: Make sure both arguments cover the same rows.

commonErrors.cause: The destination cells below the formula are not empty.
commonErrors.fix: Clear the spill range or move the formula.

name: UNIQUE

params.name: array
params.description: The range or array to de-duplicate.

params.name: by_col
params.description: TRUE compares columns instead of rows; default FALSE.

params.name: exactly_once
params.description: TRUE returns only values that appear exactly once.

summary: Returns the distinct values from a range or array.
intro: UNIQUE turns a messy list into a clean set while preserving the order values first appear. It spills the result vertically by default, and the optional exactly_once switch is a quick way to isolate values that occur only one time.

examples.title: List each name once
examples.note: UNIQUE preserves first-seen order; TEXTJOIN displays it inline.

examples.title: Count distinct numbers
examples.note: The unique values are 10 and 20.

commonErrors.cause: UNIQUE cannot return a result from an empty array.
commonErrors.fix: Check that the input range actually contains values.

commonErrors.cause: Cells below the formula are occupied.
commonErrors.fix: Clear the spill area or anchor UNIQUE in a blank column.

commonErrors.cause: Values differ by hidden spaces or case.
commonErrors.fix: Clean with TRIM and a case-normalizing function first.

name: SORT

params.name: array
params.description: The range or array to sort.

params.name: sort_index
params.description: The row or column to sort by; defaults to 1.

params.name: sort_order
params.description: 1 for ascending, -1 for descending; default ascending.

params.name: by_col
params.description: TRUE sorts by column; default FALSE sorts by row.

summary: Sorts a range or array dynamically and spills the result.
intro: SORT reorders rows without changing the source data, which makes it ideal for ranked reports and dashboards. Choose the sort column with sort_index, flip direction with -1, and remember the output is a spilled array rather than a single cell value.

examples.title: Highest sales first
examples.note: SORT orders by column 2 descending; INDEX reads the top value.

examples.title: Alphabetical labels
examples.note: Ascending order puts East first.

commonErrors.cause: sort_index points outside the array dimensions.
commonErrors.fix: Use 1 for a one-column range; for tables, count the sort column from the left.

commonErrors.cause: The output range overlaps existing data.
commonErrors.fix: Move the formula or clear the destination cells.

commonErrors.cause: SORT does not modify the input range; only the spilled copy is sorted.
commonErrors.fix: If you need the original reordered, copy the spilled result and paste values.

name: CHOOSE

params.name: index_num
params.description: The 1-based position of the value to return.

params.name: value1
params.description: The first possible value.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional possible values, up to 254 total.

summary: Returns one value from a list based on its position number.
intro: CHOOSE is a compact selector: give it a position and a list of candidates, and it returns the candidate at that position. It is often used inside other formulas to switch ranges, labels or calculation branches without nested IFs.

examples.title: Choose a medal label
examples.note: The index is a position, not a lookup key.

commonErrors.cause: index_num is less than 1 or greater than the number of values supplied.
commonErrors.fix: Clamp the index with MIN/MAX or supply a matching number of choices.

commonErrors.cause: The list order does not match the business numbering.
commonErrors.fix: Number choices from 1 in the exact order the index expects.

commonErrors.cause: index_num is text such as "2" rather than a number.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the source in VALUE or ensure the cell is numeric.

name: OFFSET

params.name: reference
params.description: The starting cell or range.

params.name: rows
params.description: Rows to move up or down; negative moves up.

params.name: cols
params.description: Columns to move left or right; negative moves left.

params.name: height
params.description: Height of the returned range; defaults to reference height.

params.name: width
params.description: Width of the returned range; defaults to reference width.

summary: Returns a reference shifted from a starting cell by rows and columns.
intro: OFFSET is a moving pointer: start at a cell, shift it, and optionally resize the window it points to. It powers flexible totals and lookups, but it is volatile and easy to break when rows are inserted, so prefer structured references or INDEX for new workbooks.

examples.title: Sum a shifted column
examples.note: From A1, move one column right and take three rows: B1:B3.

examples.title: Sum a two-column window
examples.note: The window B2:C3 contains 2, 3, 5 and 6.

commonErrors.cause: The shifted range falls outside the worksheet.
commonErrors.fix: Check rows/cols signs and keep the anchor far enough from edges.

commonErrors.cause: OFFSET is volatile and can slow large workbooks.
commonErrors.fix: Replace with INDEX or a fixed range where possible.

commonErrors.error: Returns a reference, not a value
commonErrors.cause: OFFSET alone displays the upper-left cell of the shifted range.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap it in SUM, AVERAGE, INDEX or another function.

name: SUMPRODUCT

params.name: array1
params.description: The first array or range to multiply.

params.name: array2
params.description: Additional arrays of the same dimensions.

summary: Multiplies corresponding items in arrays and sums the products.
intro: SUMPRODUCT is the workhorse behind weighted totals, conditional sums and matrix-style calculations. It pairs each value in one range with the same position in another, multiplies them, and adds the results — no helper column required.

examples.title: Sum only larger quantities
examples.note: The Boolean test zeroes out the quantity-1 row, so only 5 + 8 = 13 counts.

commonErrors.cause: Array arguments have different dimensions.
commonErrors.fix: Make every range the same number of rows and columns.

commonErrors.cause: Text or blanks inside a numeric array can be treated as zero in some constructions.
commonErrors.fix: Clean the source range or use explicit numeric tests.

commonErrors.cause: Long Boolean expressions are easy to misread.
commonErrors.fix: Break the condition into a helper column when clarity matters more than compactness.

name: ROUNDUP

params.name: number
params.description: The number to round.

params.name: num_digits
params.description: Digits to keep; negative values round to tens, hundreds and so on.

summary: Rounds a number away from zero.
intro: ROUNDUP always moves the value farther from zero: 3.21 becomes 3.3 at one digit, and 1234 becomes 1300 at minus two digits. It is the conservative choice for ceilings, budgets and capacity estimates where you never want to understate.

examples.title: Round up to hundreds
examples.note: A negative digit count rounds left of the decimal point.

commonErrors.cause: ROUNDUP ignores the next digit and always rounds away from zero.
commonErrors.fix: Use ROUND when you need nearest-value rounding.

commonErrors.cause: ROUNDUP(-1.2,0) returns -2, not -1.
commonErrors.fix: Check the sign before applying it to credits or adjustments.

commonErrors.cause: num_digits is text rather than a number.
commonErrors.fix: Remove quotes or convert the cell with VALUE.

name: ROUNDDOWN

params.name: number
params.description: The number to round.

params.name: num_digits
params.description: Digits to keep; negative values round to tens, hundreds and so on.

summary: Rounds a number toward zero.
intro: ROUNDDOWN truncates toward zero no matter what the discarded digits are: 3.99 stays below 4 at zero digits, and 1234 becomes 1200 at minus two digits. It is the floor for positive values and the ceiling for negatives, which makes it useful for conservative allocations.

commonErrors.cause: ROUNDDOWN truncates even when the next digit is 9.
commonErrors.fix: Use ROUND for nearest-value rounding.

commonErrors.cause: ROUNDDOWN(-1.9,0) returns -1.
commonErrors.fix: Verify whether the business rule wants toward zero or true floor.

commonErrors.cause: num_digits is not numeric.
commonErrors.fix: Pass a number or a cell containing a number.

name: MOD

params.name: number
params.description: The number to divide.

params.name: divisor
params.description: The number to divide by.

summary: Returns the remainder after division.
intro: MOD answers 'what is left over' after integer-style division. It is the clean way to test even/odd values, cycle through weekday or month patterns, and extract the last digits of an ID without text functions.

examples.title: Last digit of an ID
examples.note: The remainder after dividing by 10 is the ones digit.

commonErrors.cause: The divisor is zero.
commonErrors.fix: Guard the formula with IF(divisor=0,...) or fix the source cell.

commonErrors.cause: Excel's MOD result takes the sign of the divisor, not always the dividend.
commonErrors.fix: For mathematical modulo on negatives, adjust with the divisor sign.

commonErrors.cause: MOD is not limited to integers.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap in INT or ROUND if you expected whole-number behavior.

name: RANK

params.name: number
params.description: The value whose rank you want.

params.name: ref
params.description: The range of values to rank against.

params.name: order
params.description: 0 or omitted for descending, 1 for ascending.

summary: Returns the rank of a number within a list of numbers.
intro: RANK places a value in order inside a range and returns its position, with ties sharing the same rank. It is the classic way to answer 'where does this score sit?' without sorting the source data first.

examples.title: Rank a score, highest first
examples.note: Only 95 ranks higher.

examples.title: Rank smallest first
examples.note: Ascending order makes 64 the leader.

commonErrors.cause: The number is not present in ref.
commonErrors.fix: Check for text-formatted numbers or include the value in the range.

commonErrors.cause: Equal values receive the same position and skip the next rank.
commonErrors.fix: Use RANK.EQ behavior intentionally or add a tiny tie-breaker column.

commonErrors.cause: Some locales prefer RANK.EQ or RANK.AVG.
commonErrors.fix: Use RANK.EQ for the same descending default with clearer naming.

name: AND

params.name: logical1
params.description: The first condition to test.

params.name: logical2
params.description: Additional conditions; all must be TRUE for AND to return TRUE.

summary: Returns TRUE only when every condition is TRUE.
intro: AND is the all-must-pass gate: use it for eligibility rules, minimum-score checks and multi-criteria approvals. It ignores text and empty cells inside ranges, but if no logical value exists at all it returns #VALUE!.

examples.title: Inside an IF gate
examples.note: One failing condition sends the whole AND to FALSE.

commonErrors.cause: No argument contains a logical value.
commonErrors.fix: Make sure at least one test compares numbers, text or dates.

commonErrors.cause: AND skips text and blanks when scanning a range.
commonErrors.fix: Convert intended text tests into explicit comparisons.

commonErrors.cause: A zero or blank used as a direct argument counts as FALSE.
commonErrors.fix: Replace blanks with explicit TRUE/FALSE logic where needed.

name: OR

params.name: logical1
params.description: The first condition to test.

params.name: logical2
params.description: Additional conditions; any TRUE result makes OR return TRUE.

summary: Returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE.
intro: OR is the any-one-is-enough gate: perfect for 'flag if any threshold is breached' checks, fallback eligibility and exception reporting. Like AND, it ignores text in ranges and returns #VALUE! when it cannot find a logical value.

examples.title: Any low score flags review
examples.note: The first condition is TRUE, so OR stops caring about the second.

commonErrors.cause: The arguments contain no logical values.
commonErrors.fix: Use comparison operators such as >, <, = or <> inside OR.

commonErrors.cause: One broad condition is enough to trigger the whole OR.
commonErrors.fix: Tighten each test or split the rule into separate checks.

commonErrors.cause: Empty cells in a range do not count as FALSE or TRUE.
commonErrors.fix: Use COUNTBLANK or an explicit blank test when blanks matter.

name: NOT

params.name: logical
params.description: The condition to reverse.

summary: Reverses a logical value: TRUE becomes FALSE and FALSE becomes TRUE.
intro: NOT is the inversion switch for formulas that read more naturally as 'not blank', 'not found' or 'outside range'. It takes exactly one logical test, so nest it inside IF or combine it with AND/OR for compound rules.

examples.title: Reverse a threshold test
examples.note: 90 is greater than 80, so the original test is TRUE and NOT flips it.

examples.title: Detect a non-empty cell
examples.note: TRIM turns the space into an empty string, making the inner test TRUE.

commonErrors.cause: The argument is text that cannot be interpreted as a logical value.
commonErrors.fix: Use a comparison such as A1="" inside NOT.

commonErrors.cause: NOT(NOT(...)) cancels itself out.
commonErrors.fix: Simplify the expression instead of stacking negations.

commonErrors.cause: The original condition already returns the opposite of what you expect.
commonErrors.fix: Test the inner comparison by itself before wrapping it in NOT.

name: SWITCH

params.name: expression
params.description: The value to compare against each case.

params.name: value1
params.description: The first case value to match.

params.name: result1
params.description: The result returned when value1 matches.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional case/result pairs.

params.name: default
params.description: Optional fallback when nothing matches.

summary: Compares a value against a list and returns the first matching result.
intro: SWITCH is a cleaner multi-way branch than nested IFs: list expression once, then case/result pairs in order. It performs exact matching, stops at the first hit, and can end with a default so unexpected values do not leak #N/A into reports.

commonErrors.cause: No case matches and no default was supplied.
commonErrors.fix: Add a final default value after the last result.

commonErrors.cause: SWITCH text matching is not case-insensitive by default in all contexts.
commonErrors.fix: Normalize both sides with UPPER or LOWER before switching.

commonErrors.cause: Every value needs a result; a dangling value causes an error or wrong output.
commonErrors.fix: Count arguments in pairs before the optional default.

name: MEDIAN

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range to evaluate.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges.

summary: Returns the middle value of a set of numbers.
intro: MEDIAN finds the center of a distribution without being dragged by outliers the way AVERAGE can. With an odd count it returns the middle number; with an even count it averages the two middle values, making it the right quick robust average for salaries, scores and durations.

examples.title: Even-count median
examples.note: The middle two values 20 and 30 are averaged.

commonErrors.cause: The range contains no numeric values.
commonErrors.fix: Check that cells are numbers rather than text.

commonErrors.cause: MEDIAN ignores text and blanks, which can hide missing data.
commonErrors.fix: Use COUNT or COUNTA alongside it to confirm coverage.

commonErrors.cause: MEDIAN is positional, not the most frequent value.
commonErrors.fix: Use MODE.SNGL for the most common value.

name: PERCENTILE.INC

params.name: array
params.description: The range of numbers to evaluate.

params.name: k
params.description: The percentile as a decimal from 0 to 1.

summary: Returns the k-th percentile of values using inclusive interpolation.
intro: PERCENTILE.INC answers questions like 'what score sits at the 90th percentile?' by interpolating between sorted values. k is a fraction, not a whole percent: 0.9 means the 90th percentile, and the result falls between data points when the percentile lands off a rank.

examples.title: Ninetieth percentile
examples.note: The position falls between 40 and 50, giving 46.

commonErrors.cause: k is less than 0 or greater than 1.
commonErrors.fix: Pass a decimal fraction such as 0.75, not 75.

commonErrors.cause: The array contains text that cannot be evaluated.
commonErrors.fix: Clean or convert the source range first.

commonErrors.cause: PERCENTILE.INC returns a value between observations rather than an observed value.
commonErrors.fix: Use PERCENTILE.EXC or QUARTILE for a different boundary convention.

name: YEAR

params.name: serial_number
params.description: A date or date serial number.

summary: Returns the year of a date as a four-digit number.
intro: YEAR extracts just the year component from any date Excel understands, which makes it the simplest way to group records by year or validate that a date falls in the expected period. It returns a number, so it can be compared, summed or used in further date formulas.

commonErrors.cause: The cell contains text Excel cannot recognize as a date.
commonErrors.fix: Use DATEVALUE or fix the source format first.

commonErrors.cause: A date like 1/2/26 may be interpreted in the 2020s or 1900s depending on settings.
commonErrors.fix: Enter four-digit years in source data.

commonErrors.cause: YEAR returns a number but the cell may inherit date formatting.
commonErrors.fix: Set the result cell to General or Number.

name: MONTH

params.name: serial_number
params.description: A date or date serial number.

summary: Returns the month of a date as a number from 1 to 12.
intro: MONTH pulls the calendar month out of a date serial, which is exactly what you need for month-over-month comparisons, fiscal labels and grouping. Like YEAR, the result is numeric and ignores any time portion attached to the date.

commonErrors.cause: The argument is not a valid date.
commonErrors.fix: Convert text dates with DATEVALUE or repair the source.

commonErrors.cause: MONTH uses the date part only.
commonErrors.fix: No action needed; this is usually the desired behavior.

commonErrors.cause: MONTH returns 1-12, not 'Jan' or 'January'.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap it in TEXT or CHOOSE for a label.

name: EOMONTH

params.name: start_date
params.description: Any date inside the starting month.

params.name: months
params.description: Months to move before returning the last day; negative moves backward.

summary: Returns the last day of the month offset by a number of months.
intro: EOMONTH is the reliable way to land on a month-end without counting days yourself. Billing cycles, depreciation schedules and 'due at month end' rules all use the same pattern: anchor on any day in the month, then ask for the final date.

commonErrors.cause: start_date is text Excel cannot parse.
commonErrors.fix: Use DATE or DATEVALUE to build a real date first.

commonErrors.cause: The requested date is outside Excel's supported range.
commonErrors.fix: Use smaller month offsets or check the source year.

commonErrors.cause: The result is a date serial and may display oddly if the cell was formatted as text.
commonErrors.fix: Format the cell as a date.

name: WORKDAY

params.name: start_date
params.description: The date to start counting from.

params.name: days
params.description: Working days to add; negative counts backward.

params.name: holidays
params.description: Optional range of non-working dates to exclude.

summary: Returns a date that is a given number of working days away.
intro: WORKDAY skips Saturdays and Sundays automatically and can skip a holiday list you supply. It is the standard function for SLA dates, payment terms and project deadlines expressed as 'five business days from today'.

examples.title: Five business days from Friday
examples.note: The weekend of Nov 14-15 is skipped.

examples.title: Skip a holiday
examples.note: Monday Nov 16 is excluded as a holiday.

commonErrors.cause: start_date or a holiday entry is not a valid date.
commonErrors.fix: Clean holiday cells so they contain dates, not text.

commonErrors.cause: WORKDAY always assumes Saturday/Sunday weekends.
commonErrors.fix: Use WORKDAY.INTL for custom weekend patterns.

commonErrors.cause: days is so large the result leaves Excel's date range.
commonErrors.fix: Reduce the offset or verify the start date.

name: ISERROR

params.name: value
params.description: The value or formula result to test.

summary: Returns TRUE if a value is any Excel error.
intro: ISERROR is the broad error detector: it catches #N/A, #VALUE!, #REF!, #DIV/0!, #NUM!, #NAME? and #NULL!. Use it to branch around fragile formulas, but prefer IFERROR when you simply want a fallback value instead of a TRUE/FALSE flag.

examples.title: Detect a bad conversion
examples.note: VALUE cannot convert letters, so the result is an error.

commonErrors.cause: ISERROR returns TRUE for every error, so you cannot tell #N/A from #DIV/0!.
commonErrors.fix: Use ISNA, ISERR or ISNUMBER depending on the case.

commonErrors.cause: It only reports the error; the underlying formula still needs fixing.
commonErrors.fix: Pair it with IFERROR or fix the source reference.

commonErrors.cause: A referenced cell already contains an error value.
commonErrors.fix: Trace precedents and repair the first failing cell.

name: ISBLANK

params.name: value
params.description: The cell or value to test.

summary: Returns TRUE only when a cell is truly empty.
intro: ISBLANK distinguishes an untouched cell from cells that merely look empty. A cell containing a space, a formula returning "", or a zero is not blank, which makes ISBLANK the precise tool for validating required fields and spotting missing imports.

examples.title: Space is not blank
examples.note: A single space makes the cell non-empty; use TRIM if spaces should count as blank.

commonErrors.cause: ISBLANK looks at the cell content, not the displayed result.
commonErrors.fix: Use =A1="" or LEN(TRIM(A1))=0 for formula-generated empties.

commonErrors.cause: A numeric 0 is a real value.
commonErrors.fix: Test ISNUMBER separately when zero should be treated as missing.

commonErrors.cause: ISBLANK expects a reference in normal use.
commonErrors.fix: Point it at a cell rather than a literal unless you intentionally test an expression.

name: LET

params.name: name1
params.description: The first name to assign; must follow Excel name rules.

params.name: value1
params.description: The value stored in name1.

params.name: calculation
params.description: The final expression that uses the names.

summary: Defines named values inside a formula and returns the final calculation.
intro: LET makes long formulas readable by letting you name intermediate values once and reuse them in the final calculation. It reduces repeated range scans, documents intent inside the formula itself, and is the foundation for cleaner modern Excel models.

commonErrors.cause: The workbook runs in Excel 2019 or earlier, which lacks LET.
commonErrors.fix: Rewrite the calculation without named values or upgrade Excel.

commonErrors.cause: A name conflicts with a cell reference or is misspelled in the calculation.
commonErrors.fix: Use unique names that cannot be mistaken for A1-style references.

commonErrors.cause: Every name needs a value before the final calculation.
commonErrors.fix: Count name/value pairs; the last argument is the calculation, not a value.
